section.title: The Day of the LORD and His Reign
section.sectionRationale: The book ends where all history is heading. The nations gather one last time against Jerusalem, but the LORD Himself goes out to fight, and His feet stand on the Mount of Olives. Living waters flow from the city, and the LORD becomes King over all the earth, the LORD alone and His name alone. In the end even the horses' bells and the cooking pots are inscribed Holy to the LORD. Zechariah closes with the whole world made a temple.
section.thesis: The LORD Himself will come to defeat His enemies, reign as King over all the earth, and make all things holy, so that the whole of life becomes worship and His name alone is exalted.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the city taken yet rescued as the LORD stands on the split Mount of Olives; the unique day of living waters and the LORD as King alone; the plague on the nations and the wealth gathered in; and the survivors coming up to worship at Tabernacles, until every pot in Jerusalem is Holy to the LORD.

units.label: The LORD stands on the Mount of Olives
units.note: the city rescued by God Himself

verses.text: Behold, a {{yom|day}} of the LORD is coming when your plunder will be divided in your presence.

For I will gather all the nations for battle against Jerusalem, and the city will be captured, the houses looted, and the women ravished. Half of the city will go into exile, but the rest of the people will not be removed from the city.
Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations, as He fights in the day of battle.

On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and the Mount of Olives will be split in two from east to west, forming a great valley, with half the mountain moving to the north and half to the south.

You will flee by My mountain valley, for it will extend to Azal. You will flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him.

units.label: Living waters and the King over all the earth
units.note: the LORD alone, and His name alone

verses.text: On that day there will be no light, no cold or frost.
It will be a unique day known only to the LORD, without day or night; but when evening comes, there will be light.
And on that day {{chayyim|living water}} will flow out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the Eastern Sea and the other half toward the Western Sea, in summer and winter alike.
On that day the LORD will become {{melek|King}} over all the earth, the LORD {{echad|alone}}, and His name alone.

All the land from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem will be turned into a plain, but Jerusalem will be raised up and will remain in her place, from the Benjamin Gate to the site of the First Gate to the Corner Gate, and from the Tower of Hananel to the royal winepresses.
People will live there, and never again will there be an utter destruction. So Jerusalem will dwell securely.

And this will be the plague with which the LORD strikes all the peoples who have warred against Jerusalem: Their flesh will rot while they stand on their feet, their eyes will rot in their sockets, and their tongues will rot in their mouths.
On that day a great panic from the LORD will come upon them, so that each will seize the hand of another, and the hand of one will rise against the other.
Judah will also fight at Jerusalem, and the wealth of all the surrounding nations will be collected, gold, silver, and apparel in great abundance.
And a similar plague will strike the horses and mules, camels and donkeys, and all the animals in those camps.
Then all the survivors from the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
And should any of the families of the earth not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, then the rain will not fall on them.

And if the people of Egypt will not go up and enter in, then the rain will not fall on them; this will be the plague with which the LORD strikes the nations who do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
This will be the punishment of Egypt and of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
On that day, {{qodesh|HOLY}} TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses, and the cooking pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar.

Indeed, every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of Hosts, and all who sacrifice will come and take some pots and cook in them. And on that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts.

yom.gloss: The day of the LORD, the appointed time when God breaks into history to judge His enemies and save His people. The prophets use it for both near acts of judgment and the final, decisive day. Zechariah's last chapter gathers up the theme: a single climactic day of battle, rescue, and universal reign, when God settles all accounts and takes the throne over all the earth.

chayyim.gloss: Living water, water that flows and gives life, as from a spring rather than a stagnant cistern. From Jerusalem it streams east and west, summer and winter alike, never failing. The image runs from Eden's rivers to Ezekiel's temple stream to the river of life in Revelation, and Jesus claims it for Himself as the giver of living water by the Spirit.

melek.gloss: King, sovereign ruler. The climax of the book is that the LORD becomes King over all the earth, not merely over Israel. His kingship, long confessed by faith, is at last made visible and universal, every rival throne removed, so that His reign is acknowledged everywhere and forever.

echad.gloss: One, alone, undivided. The word echoes the Shema, the LORD is one. On that day the LORD will be one and His name one: no idols beside Him, no divided worship, no rival names. The confession of Israel's faith becomes the confession of all the earth, God alone acknowledged and His name alone exalted.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, that which is set apart for God. The inscription on the high priest's turban, Holy to the LORD, is now stamped on the bells of ordinary horses and the common cooking pots. The line between sacred and secular dissolves; all of life is consecrated, the whole city a temple, every ordinary thing fit for the worship of God.

basic.context: Zechariah closes with the day of the LORD. The nations gather one final time against Jerusalem, and the city suffers terribly, half of it going into exile. But then the LORD Himself goes out to fight, and His feet stand on the Mount of Olives, splitting it in two to make a way of escape. A unique day dawns with no ordinary night, living waters flow from the city to both seas, and the LORD becomes King over all the earth, the LORD alone and His name alone. The nations that warred are struck with plague, yet the survivors come up to worship the King at the Feast of Tabernacles, until even the horses' bells and the cooking pots are inscribed Holy to the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This is apocalyptic prophecy of the day of the LORD, full of vivid imagery. Believers differ on how literally to read the split mountain, the living waters, and the temple worship at Tabernacles. Some expect a literal future reign centered on Jerusalem; others read the images as a picture of Christ's final triumph and the new creation. All agree on the core: the LORD Himself comes, He reigns as King over all, and all things are made holy.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is framed by the yom, the day of the LORD, God's decisive breaking into history. From Jerusalem flow mayim chayyim, living waters, ever-flowing to both seas. The LORD becomes melek, King, over all the earth, and He is echad, one and alone, no rival gods or names beside Him, echoing the Shema. And at the last, qodesh, Holy to the LORD, the words from the high priest's turban, are stamped on horses' bells and cooking pots.
basic.typology: The LORD standing on the Mount of Olives answers the promise that the same Jesus who ascended from there will return in like manner. The living waters flowing from Jerusalem fulfill Ezekiel's temple river and the living water Jesus gives by the Spirit, consummated in Revelation's river of life. The universal reign of the King alone is fulfilled in Christ, to whom every knee will bow.
basic.christ: The LORD who comes to fight, stands on the Mount of Olives, and reigns as King is the God whom the New Testament reveals in Jesus Christ. From the Mount of Olives Jesus ascended, and the angels promised He would return the same way. He is the giver of living water and the King before whom every knee will bow, so that the LORD alone, His name alone, is the exaltation of the Lamb who was slain now enthroned over all.
basic.god: God is the divine Warrior who fights for His people, the King who takes His throne over all the earth, and the Holy One who makes even the common things sacred. He is jealous for His name: on that day there are no rival gods and no divided worship. Yet His triumph is not mere conquest; it opens into a world watered by living streams, secure from destruction, where the nations that once attacked now come to worship, and every ordinary thing is consecrated to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 1:11 promises Jesus will return as He left, from the Mount of Olives. Ezekiel 47 and Revelation 22 show the life-giving river from God's presence. Revelation 11:15 announces the kingdom of the world become the kingdom of our Lord. Philippians 2 says every knee will bow to Jesus.
basic.oneStory: The whole of Scripture drives toward the day when God reigns unopposed and all creation is holy. Zechariah's final chapter shows the LORD coming to fight, standing on the Mount of Olives, pouring out living waters, and being crowned King over all the earth, alone. It is fulfilled in Christ, who ascended from that mountain, gives the water of life, and will return to reign, making the whole world a temple where His name alone is exalted.

context.literary:
Chapter 14 is built as a sequence of scenes, each opened by "on that day" or by "then," and the order of the scenes is the argument. Verses 1 to 5 show the worst: the city taken, houses looted, half the people carried off. Verses 3 to 5 reverse it at once with the LORD going out to fight, so the section reads like a descent and a rescue in a single breath. Verses 6 to 11 shift from battlefield to cosmos: the sky, the seasons, the rivers, the land itself are remade, and the passage reaches its summit at verse 9, "the LORD alone, and His name alone." Verses 12 to 15 return to the enemies and describe their undoing in a horrifying close-up, and verses 16 to 21 move to the aftermath, which is worship.

The chapter has a clear symmetry in its geography. It begins with the nations inside Jerusalem's walls (verse 2) and ends with the nations coming up to its feast (verse 16). It begins with plunder divided in the city (verse 1) and ends with every pot in the city holy (verse 21). It begins with flight from the city (verse 5) and ends with pilgrimage to it. In between, the Mount of Olives splits to make a way out, and the land around becomes a plain while Jerusalem is raised.

The final verses use the language of the temple to describe all of life. The inscription "HOLY TO THE LORD," once on the high priest's turban, is found on horse bells, and the common cooking pot is placed on a level with the bowls before the altar. The prophecy ends not with a battle but with the removal of the border between sacred and ordinary, a quiet and total conclusion to the book, and, in the order of the Christian canon, the last prophecy before Malachi.
context.historical:
To those who first heard this, Jerusalem was a modest provincial town. Its temple was a plain building beside the memory of Solomon's, and its walls were thin. The vision begins with the opposite of reassurance. The city is captured, women are ravished (14:2), and half the people go into exile. The community could remember a day like it, and some of them had lived through the Babylonian destruction. Zechariah does not pretend the future will be soft, and that honesty makes the rescue credible.

Some features of the scene point to real geography. The Mount of Olives rises to the east of the city across the Kidron valley, and from its ridge one looks down on the temple mount. A great valley running east to west would open an escape route toward the Dead Sea basin, the "Eastern Sea" of verse 8. The Western Sea is the Mediterranean. The place called Azal in verse 5 is not otherwise known, and the Hebrew of that verse is difficult. The mention of the earthquake in Uzziah's days points to a famous shaking that Amos 1:1 uses to date the ministry of Amos, and that was still remembered two centuries later.

Verse 10 draws a circle of land from Geba, on Judah's northern edge, to Rimmon in the south. Turning that high country into a plain makes Jerusalem the only height, which is how the prophets say the mountain of the LORD's house will stand in the last days (Isaiah 2:2, Micah 4:1). The list of gates and towers fixes the city's bounds in terms the hearers knew.

The Feast of Tabernacles was the autumn harvest pilgrimage, when families lived in booths for a week (Leviticus 23:33-43, Deuteronomy 16:13-15). It was the feast of rain and of thanksgiving, which makes the threat for neglecting it, no rain, a fitting one. Egypt is named because its crops depend on the Nile and not on rain, so even a nation that seems exempt is not.
context.canonical:
Zechariah 14 pulls together threads from nearly every prophet. The nations gathered for battle recall Joel 3:2, 9-16 and Ezekiel 38 and 39. The earthquake and the cosmic disturbance echo Isaiah 24 and Joel 2:10. The living water that flows from the temple area to both seas is a close relative of Ezekiel 47:1-12, where a river flows from the threshold of the temple east toward the Dead Sea, bringing life, and of Joel 3:18. The picture of the nations coming up to Jerusalem to worship is found in Isaiah 2:2-4 and 66:23, and in Zechariah 8:20-23.

The New Testament hears the chapter in several places. Jesus's ascension from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:11-12) is followed by the angels' promise that He will return in the same way. In the Olivet discourse He speaks of darkened skies and the Son of Man coming on the clouds (Matthew 24:29-30), and Matthew 25:31 pictures His coming with all the angels. Paul speaks of the coming of the Lord Jesus with all His saints (1 Thessalonians 3:13), echoing "all the holy ones with Him" in verse 5. John 7:37-38 sets Jesus' invitation to drink on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the very feast of this chapter, and Revelation draws on its images repeatedly: the river of life (22:1-2), a day with no night (21:25; 22:5), no more curse (22:3), and the kingdom of the world become the kingdom of our Lord (11:15).

The last line of the Old Testament in Christian order, Malachi 4:6, ends with the word cherem, the ban or curse. Zechariah 14:11 promises that there will never again be cherem on Jerusalem. The book that stands before it closes the account on a note that the next book's final word seems to answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah meant the final chapter to carry a small and anxious people through the long wait. They were being told that the story did not end in the ordinary way, with the strongest army, and that the story would end with God alone as King. The promise of a terrible day for Jerusalem is not given to terrify but to hold their eyes on the other side of it: whatever the city suffers, the LORD Himself will go out, and His coming will end the fighting.

He also meant the hearers to understand that the final goal is not a purified Israel standing apart from the nations. It is a world in which the nations that came to attack come to worship. The survivors go up year after year to the King. The line between Israel and the rest, and between the temple and the kitchen, is erased by consecration and not by conquest. The prophet wants his hearers to live now in the light of a world in which everything is "holy to the LORD," and to let that expectation shape their worship and their ordinary work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a description of what God will do. No command is addressed to the hearers except the quiet one implied in the whole chapter: wait for the King and worship Him. The graphic details of the plague on the nations' flesh and animals should not be turned into a rule for how any believer treats an enemy; they describe God's own judgment and are not an instruction.

What is meant to carry over is the shape of the hope. The holiness that reaches to horse bells and cooking pots tells believers that no part of life is outside God's claim, a conviction echoed in 1 Corinthians 10:31, "So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God." The practice of going up to worship the King is also taken as a model of how the nations are drawn to God, not by compulsion but by sight of His reign. And the promise that the day belongs to the LORD, known only to Him (verse 7), is a reminder that the timing is not ours to compute.

debates.question: How literally should the chapter be read?

views.label: A literal future, centered on Jerusalem
views.case: Read straightforwardly, the split Mount of Olives, the siege, the living waters and the nations going up to the Feast describe a real future era in which Christ reigns from a restored Jerusalem over the nations. Acts 1:11-12 ties the return to the same mountain, and the details of the geography are given with precision.

views.label: Apocalyptic imagery of Christ's final triumph and the new creation
views.case: The pictures portray in Old Testament temple language the return of Christ, the life He gives by the Spirit and the new heaven and earth of Revelation 21 and 22. On this view Jerusalem, Tabernacles and the temple vessels are the vocabulary of worship, in which the church and the nations are now drawn to Christ and in which the final state has no temple at all (Revelation 21:22).

debates.bearing: Both agree on the center: the LORD Himself comes, reigns as King alone, and makes all things holy. The disagreement is over how much of the furniture is meant to be taken as a map and how much as a picture.

debates.question: Why does worship at the Feast of Tabernacles, with sacrifices, appear in the final age?

views.label: Literal worship in a future temple
views.case: Some hold that animal sacrifices, as in verses 16 and 21, will be restored in a future temple as memorials looking back to Christ's finished work, as the Lord's Supper looks back now.

views.label: The language of the old covenant for the worship of the new
views.case: Others point out that Hebrews says there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:18) and read the feast and the sacrifices as the only vocabulary the prophet had for universal worship, a picture of every nation gathering to the King, as in Revelation 7:9-10 where the multitude holds palm branches.

debates.bearing: All sides agree that verse 21's removal of the barrier between sacred and common is a promise of complete consecration, and that the cross is the only ground of any worship.

debates.question: Does the siege of Jerusalem belong to a past event or to a final one?

views.label: A final, end-time battle
views.case: The scale (all the nations), the cosmic changes, and the reign that follows have no historical match, so the chapter must belong to the last days.

views.label: A prophetic pattern with partial fulfillments in history
views.case: Others point to the capture of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus foretold (Luke 21:20-24), as one fulfillment of a pattern of judgment and rescue, with a final one still to come. This reading sees the nations language as typical and the final sweep as reserved for Christ's return.

debates.bearing: The chapter's own refrain, a day of the LORD, is flexible enough to hold both. Its final goal, God's undivided reign, is common ground.

study.originalLanguages:
Yom, "day," in a distinctive sense (14:1, 7). "A day of the LORD" belongs to the prophets' vocabulary for the time when God steps into history to judge and to save (Isaiah 2:12, Joel 2:1, Amos 5:18-20). Verse 7 adds that it is a day "known only to the LORD," a phrase that in Hebrew calls it a unique day, one that stands apart from the ordinary run of days and nights, with light "when evening comes." The world's rhythm is interrupted and then resumed in a way only God controls.

Mayim chayyim, "living water" (14:8). Living water means moving water, a spring or river, as opposed to a still cistern (Genesis 26:19, Song of Songs 4:15). The prophet also adds that it runs "in summer and winter alike," which in a land of seasonal streams is a sign of the miraculous: most streambeds in Judah are dry through the summer. Jeremiah 2:13 calls the LORD Himself the fountain of living waters.

Echad, "one" or "alone" (14:9). The verse says the LORD will be echad and His name echad. It is the word of the Shema, "the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), applied here to the reign of the LORD in the whole earth. The Shema's confession becomes the world's. Not only will the LORD be the one God, but His name will be the only name that is invoked. The doubling of "the LORD alone, and His name alone" removes every other claim to worship.

Cherem, "utter destruction" (14:11). This is the word for the ban placed on a city devoted to destruction (Joshua 6:17-21), and for the curse that falls on those who break covenant. Zechariah promises that Jerusalem will never again be placed under it. A city that had known siege and destruction is promised permanent safety.

Qodesh laYHWH, "HOLY TO THE LORD" (14:20). It is the inscription on the gold plate on the high priest's turban (Exodus 28:36-38). The verse says it will be on the bells of the horses. A horse was the warhorse of the world's empires (Psalm 20:7), an emblem of human strength, and the bells are the smallest part of its harness. In verse 21 the cooking pots are said to be like the sprinkling bowls (mizraq) before the altar, the vessels used to catch the blood of the sacrifices.

The last word of the book, kena'ani, is rendered "Canaanite" in the BSB, with a note "or merchant." Both senses are attested, since in Hebrew the word can mean a trader (Proverbs 31:24), and the verse may mean that no more peddling will be done in the LORD's house. The ambiguity is old, and both meanings point to a house cleared of what is foreign to it.

typology.type: The LORD's feet on the Mount of Olives
typology.fulfillment: The ridge where the LORD's feet will stand is the one from which Jesus ascended, Acts 1:9-12, and from which He had come down to the city in the triumphal entry, Luke 19:37. The angels promise He will return in the same way. The escalation is from a geographic detail to a person: the God who fights is the one the disciples watched rise. The type falls short in one respect, since the passage speaks of a LORD whose arrival splits the earth, while the first coming came quietly to a manger. The two arrivals together complete the picture.

Ezekiel's river from the temple threshold, Ezekiel 47:1-12, and Zechariah's living waters find their answer in the invitation Jesus gave at the Feast of Tabernacles, John 7:37-39, where He offers streams of living water, which John says is the Spirit. They end in the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1-2. The fulfillment is not a stream out of a building but out of a person. The type falls short because the prophets' water flowed from a temple, and in the end there is no temple, only the throne.

typology.type: The LORD alone as King over all the earth
typology.fulfillment: Christ is the King who rules over the nations, Psalm 2, and the day is coming when every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, Philippians 2:10-11, and the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15. The Shema's one God is shown to be the Father with the Son, and 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 describes the handing over of the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all. The type is incomplete in that Zechariah has no word for the Son. The New Testament supplies the name.

typology.type: Holy to the LORD on the bells and the pots
typology.fulfillment: What belonged only to the high priest's turban is spread to ordinary life. In Christ, believers are called a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5 and 9, and Revelation 1:6 says He made us a kingdom of priests to serve His God. Paul takes the same pattern into daily eating and drinking in 1 Corinthians 10:31. The fulfillment goes beyond objects to people: those once called common are consecrated. The type falls short in that the pots are made holy by decree, whereas people are made holy by new birth and the Spirit's work.

study.christ:
Most of this chapter is about the LORD, and the New Testament says that the LORD is the one who came in Jesus. Nothing in the chapter makes a separate promise of a Messiah; instead the Messiah is hidden in the person of God. "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him" (verse 5), and the one who comes is the Lord Jesus coming "with all His saints" (1 Thessalonians 3:13) and all His angels (Matthew 25:31). The footnote in the BSB notes that the Hebrew of verse 5 says "with You," a sudden turn to address the LORD directly, as the prophet sees Him arriving and cannot keep from speaking to Him.

The most visible link is the mountain. The LORD's feet stand on the Mount of Olives, and it was from there that Jesus ascended, with the promise of the angels that "this same Jesus... will come back in the same way" (Acts 1:11). The Gospels place a series of scenes on the Olivet slope: the triumphal entry from the east (Luke 19:37), the great discourse on the end (Matthew 24:3), and the agony of Gethsemane. The one who is to stand there as warrior is the one who wept over the city from there (Luke 19:41).

The living water belongs to Christ's own words. On "the last and greatest day of the feast" (John 7:37), the day of the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus stood and cried out that anyone who was thirsty should come to Him and drink. John adds that He spoke of the Spirit. That is not a coincidence of seasons: the feast was a time when this chapter would have been in mind, and Jesus claims to be what the water pointed to. The river of Revelation 22 then flows "from the throne of God and of the Lamb," and the Lamb is given a place at the source.

The universal reign of verse 9 is the exaltation of Christ. Paul says that God has given Him the name above every name so that every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9-11), and the Shema's "the LORD is one" is spoken by Paul of the one God and the one Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The chapter's "the LORD alone" is not threatened by this reading; it is fulfilled in it.

One caution. The New Testament never quotes Zechariah 14 as a proof text, and the detailed furniture of the chapter, the plague, the Feast, the pots, should not be forced into precise one-to-one correspondences. What the apostles draw from it is its center: the Lord comes from the Mount of Olives, the water of life flows, and one King reigns over all.
study.god:
This chapter gives a portrait of God as warrior, and it is worth noticing how He fights. He does not appear until the city has been taken and half its people are in exile. He then goes out "as He fights in the day of battle" (verse 3), a phrase that points back to the Exodus and the conquests when He fought for Israel (Exodus 14:14, Deuteronomy 1:30). He wins by panic from His own hand, setting each man against his neighbor (verse 13), as He did at Gideon's spring (Judges 7:22), and by plague. His victory is not delegated, and the people He rescues have little to do but flee through the valley He opens.

The second portrait is of God as master of the created order. The Mount of Olives splits at His step. Light and cold and frost are rearranged, and day and night are suspended and then restored with the evening. Rivers run in dry seasons. The land is leveled and the city raised. This is the God of Genesis 1 returning to His own creation, with the power to alter even the rhythm of time, and it carries a lesson for worship: nothing believers see as fixed is out of His hands.

The ninth verse is the center of the doctrine of God in the chapter: the LORD becomes King over all the earth, "the LORD alone, and His name alone." God is not merely a king among kings, and not merely king of Israel. The word "become" is noticeable. The kingship has always been His by right, and the day comes when it is His in fact, with no rival claim anywhere. God's reign is both present and awaited, which is the tension Christians live in when they pray "Your kingdom come."

Judgment and mercy sit together. The plague is terrible and the withholding of rain is a real threat, but the chapter's most striking note is the survivors of the nations who go up to worship. God's judgment is not finally the destruction of the nations but their conversion, and some of the same peoples that besieged the city come to keep the feast. The God of this chapter is jealous for His name, yet He draws in those who once attacked Him.

And God is holy in a pervasive way. The sacred is not walled off from the common but extended to it, until even the cooking pot is as holy as the altar bowl. Holiness here is not a smaller and smaller circle but a widening one. It means that believers, who worship a God of this kind, should treat ordinary things as given, and ordinary work as a form of worship.

crossReferences.note: The disciples watch Jesus rise from the Mount of Olives, and two men in white promise that He will come back in the same way. Zechariah's picture of the LORD's feet on that mountain gives the promise a place, and ties the return of Jesus to the coming of the LORD.

A river flows from the temple threshold toward the east and grows deeper with every thousand cubits, healing the sea into which it flows. Zechariah's living water, flowing to the eastern and western seas, is a closely related vision, and both look to a world made fruitful by God's presence.

At the Feast of Tabernacles, the very feast the nations come to keep in Zechariah 14:16, Jesus calls the thirsty to come and drink and speaks of streams of living water, which John says refers to the Spirit. The chapter's water has become an offer.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, healing the nations. It is the end of Zechariah's living water and Ezekiel's river, and it places the Lamb at the source.

The city has no need of sun or moon, the nations walk by its light, and its gates are never shut, because there is no night. Zechariah's day with light at evening is the first glimpse of this city, where night is gone and the nations bring in their glory.

The Shema confesses that the LORD our God, the LORD, is one. Zechariah 14:9 takes the same word, echad, and gives it a global reach: the LORD will be one, and His name one, over all the earth. What Israel confessed alone, the nations will confess with them.

Paul declares that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Zechariah's universal kingship of the LORD alone finds its fullest explanation here, with the glory of the Son turning to the glory of the Father.

The gold plate engraved HOLY TO THE LORD was fastened on the high priest's turban, a mark of the one who bore the sins of the people. Zechariah 14:20 spreads the same inscription to the horse bells, so that what had marked one man marks a whole people and its ordinary things.

The mountain of the LORD's house is established as the chief of the mountains, raised above the hills, and all nations stream to it. Zechariah 14:10 pictures the surrounding land made a plain while Jerusalem stands high, and verse 16 shows the nations on pilgrimage, the same movement Isaiah saw.

At Gideon's attack the LORD set every man's sword against his companion throughout the camp. Zechariah 14:13 uses the same pattern of divine panic, in which the enemy's own hand is turned on itself. It shows the LORD fighting as He did before, with no need of a great army.

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever. It is Zechariah 14:9 heard from heaven, with the Messiah named alongside the LORD.

study.oneStory:
This chapter is where the story of the Old Testament ends, and it ends where it began. Genesis opens with God alone as the maker of the heavens and the earth, with light separated from darkness and waters gathered into seas. Zechariah 14 returns to that world and reorders it again: a day with no ordinary light, rivers that run in every season, a land made level. Creation is not abandoned but remade, and the Creator is shown to be King.

It also gathers up the nations. From Genesis 11, where the peoples were scattered from Babel, the Bible has asked how they can be brought home. God's promise to Abraham was that all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), and Zechariah's picture of the families of the earth going up to worship the King, year after year (14:16-17), is the answer. The nations come to the same city where the first promise was kept, and they come to keep the harvest feast, the feast of a people living in temporary shelters before their God.

The New Testament says how this will come. The King is Jesus. He ascended from the Mount of Olives, He poured out the Spirit as living water, and He will return as the LORD who fights. The Day of the LORD that every prophet anticipated and that Jesus' first coming began is completed at His return. The kingdom of the world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ (Revelation 11:15).

The final scene is the one with which the Bible closes. Revelation 21 and 22 show a city without a temple because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, where night is gone, where the river of life runs, where the gates are never shut and the nations walk by the light. The mourning, crying, and pain of the old order are gone (Revelation 21:4). Zechariah's last line, that every pot will be holy, is the quietest and most complete form of that promise: nothing in creation will be left outside the reach of God's glory, and every ordinary thing will be used in His worship.

quiz.q: Who goes out to fight for Jerusalem on the day of the LORD?

options.text: The LORD Himself, whose feet stand on the Mount of Olives.
options.note: Verses 3 and 4: the LORD goes out to fight and stands on the mountain.

options.text: A coalition of allied nations.
options.note: It is the LORD Himself, not human allies, who wins the victory.

options.text: Jerusalem's own army alone.
options.note: Judah fights too, but the deliverer is the LORD Himself.

options.text: No one; the city is simply destroyed.
options.note: The LORD rescues the city and reigns.

quiz.q: What is the climactic announcement of verse 9?

options.text: The LORD will be King over all the earth, the LORD alone and His name alone.
options.note: Verse 9 proclaims God's universal, exclusive reign.

options.text: Israel will rule over the surrounding nations.
options.note: It is the LORD who reigns over all, not Israel over her neighbors.

options.text: The nations will each keep their own gods.
options.note: The opposite: the LORD alone is King and His name alone remains.

options.text: The earth will be left without any king.
options.note: The LORD becomes King over all the earth.

quiz.q: What flows out from Jerusalem on that day?

options.text: Living waters, running to both seas, summer and winter alike.
options.note: Verse 8: ever-flowing living water toward the Eastern and Western Seas.

options.text: Rivers of blood from the battle.
options.note: It is life-giving water, not blood, that flows out.

options.text: Only a seasonal, drying stream.
options.note: The waters never fail, flowing in summer and winter alike.

options.text: Nothing flows from the city.
options.note: Living waters stream from Jerusalem to both seas.

quiz.q: What does it mean that even the horses' bells and cooking pots are inscribed Holy to the LORD?

options.text: All of life is consecrated; the whole city becomes a temple with nothing left common.
options.note: The high priest's inscription now marks the most ordinary things.

options.text: Only the temple vessels matter, and nothing else.
options.note: The point is the reverse: even common things are made holy.

options.text: Holiness is abolished altogether.
options.note: Holiness expands to fill everything, rather than disappearing.

options.text: The pots are declared worthless.
options.note: They are declared holy to the LORD, as sacred as the altar bowls.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament connect the Mount of Olives to Christ?

options.text: Jesus ascended from it, with the promise that He will return in the same way.
options.note: Acts 1:11-12 ties the mountain to Christ's ascension and return.

options.text: It is where the temple was rebuilt after exile.
options.note: The New Testament link is Christ's ascension and return, not a temple rebuild.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The Mount of Olives is directly tied to Jesus in Acts 1.

options.text: It is where the nations are said to be crowned.
options.note: It is the place of Christ's ascension and promised return.

questions: The LORD Himself came to fight for a city that could not save itself. Where do you need to stop fighting in your own strength and trust God to act?
The book ends with the LORD as King over all the earth, alone. What rival thrones and divided loyalties is He calling you to lay down before Him?
Living waters flow from the city that never run dry. Where are you thirsting, and how does Christ's promise of living water meet you there?
In the end, even the cooking pots are Holy to the LORD. How would it change your ordinary work and routines to see all of life as consecrated to God?
The nations that once made war end up worshiping the King. How does the promise that God will make even His enemies into worshipers shape how you pray for the world?

translationNotes.note: Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him; the holy ones are His angels or saints, the heavenly host accompanying His coming. The source reads and all the holy ones with Him, following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has with You.
The LORD alone, and His name alone renders the Hebrew the LORD will be one and His name one, echoing the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4; the point is undivided, exclusive worship of the one true God.

There will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD; the word can also mean merchant or trader, so it may point to the end of profaneness or of buying and selling in God's house, everything now made holy.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Zechariah 14:1-21. All 21 verses reproduced in order, reaching the end of the book at 14:21. footnote markers omitted from the running text.
